nameStory: This beetle earned its name "Asiatic garden beetle" because it originally comes from Asia (Japan, China, and Korea) but has become a common garden pest since arriving in North America in the 1920s. The "garden" part of its name reflects where people most often encounter it — munching on their prized flowers and vegetables during summer evenings.
description: The Asiatic garden beetle is a small, chunky brown beetle that belongs to the scarab family, the same group as dung beetles and June bugs. These oval-shaped beetles are typically chestnut brown to reddish-brown in color with a somewhat glossy appearance. Adults are most active during summer nights when they emerge to feed on leaves and flowers, often gathering around porch lights and other illuminated areas. Despite their small size, they can cause noticeable damage to garden plants and lawns.

idTips.label: Nighttime Activity
idTips.description: Look for these beetles flying around lights at night during summer — they're strongly attracted to illumination and you'll often find several clustered around porch lights or street lamps

idTips.label: Color and Shine
idTips.description: The body is chestnut brown to reddish-brown with a subtle glossy sheen that catches the light, giving it a polished appearance when viewed up close

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval and chunky with a distinctly rounded, dome-like back typical of scarab beetles — they feel solid and substantial when gently handled

idTips.label: Feeding Damage
idTips.description: Look for irregular holes chewed in flower petals and leaves, particularly on roses, dahlias, and other garden favorites — the damage often appears overnight

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: When disturbed during the day, they fly with a heavy, buzzing sound and somewhat clumsy flight pattern, often bumping into objects

habitat: Asiatic garden beetles thrive in residential gardens, parks, and landscaped areas throughout New England, particularly where there are well-maintained lawns and flower beds. They prefer areas with rich, organic soil where their grubs can develop, and are commonly found in suburban neighborhoods with mixed plantings of ornamental flowers, vegetables, and turf grass. You're most likely to encounter them in lower elevation areas with human habitation rather than wild, mountainous regions.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active, but grubs may be present in soil feeding on grass roots and organic matter. Look for brown patches in lawns that could indicate grub damage.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults emerge to feed and mate. Look for beetles flying around lights at night and feeding damage on garden plants, especially flowers and vegetables.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as they lay eggs in soil. New grubs begin developing underground, preparing for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and grubs overwinter deep in the soil. No above-ground beetle activity during this season.

funFact: These beetles are such enthusiastic night-fliers that they've been known to completely cover porch lights and outdoor dining areas on warm summer evenings, sometimes arriving in numbers so large that they sound like gentle rain hitting windows and screens.
confusionNotes: Often confused with Japanese beetles, but Asiatic garden beetles are smaller, more uniformly brown (lacking the metallic green head), and are primarily active at night rather than during the day. Memory trick: "Asiatic at night" — if you see them flying around lights after dark, they're likely Asiatic garden beetles.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "garden" beetle, this species was actually named Maladera castanea for many years before scientists realized it was the same species as Maladera formosae from Asia. The name change reflects our growing understanding of how many "new" pest species are actually well-known insects from other continents.
compareHints: As the only Maladera species established in New England, compare it to other scarab beetles like June bugs, which are larger and more active during late spring and early summer. Unlike the metallic Japanese beetle or the larger June beetles, Asiatic garden beetles maintain their modest brown coloration and smaller size, making them less conspicuous except when gathered around lights.
